title: Reactance Calculator
text:
Use the sliders below to adjust the Capacitance and Inductance and watch how the resonant frequency shifts.
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 600

from shiny import App, render, ui
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. Define the User Interface
app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    ui.input_slider("C_uF", "Capacitance (uF)", min=10, max=500, value=100, step=10),
    ui.input_slider("L_mH", "Inductance (mH)", min=1, max=50, value=10, step=1),
    ui.output_plot("reactance_plot")
)

# 2. Define the Server Logic
def server(input, output, session):
    @output
    @render.plot(alt="Reactance vs Frequency")
    def reactance_plot():
        C = input.C_uF() * 1e-6
        L = input.L_mH() * 1e-3
        
        f = np.linspace(10, 1000, 500)
        X_C = 1 / (2 * np.pi * f * C)
        X_L = 2 * np.pi * f * L
        
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
        ax.plot(f, X_C, label='Capacitive Reactance ($X_C$)', color='#0072B2', linewidth=2.5)
        ax.plot(f, X_L, label='Inductive Reactance ($X_L$)', color='#D55E00', linewidth=2.5)
        
        f_res = 1 / (2 * np.pi * np.sqrt(L * C))
        if f_res <= 1000:
            X_res = 2 * np.pi * f_res * L
            ax.plot(f_res, X_res, 'ko', markersize=8, label=f'Resonance ({f_res:.1f} Hz)')
            
        ax.set_title('Reactance vs Frequency', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
        ax.set_xlabel('Frequency (Hz)', fontsize=12)
        ax.set_ylabel('Reactance (Ohms)', fontsize=12)
        ax.set_ylim(0, 150)
        ax.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.7)
        ax.legend(fontsize=11)
        
        return fig

app = App(app_ui, server)

title: Project 2: Automating the Web
text:
Welcome to the Papillon Engineering K-12 Outreach Hub. This project introduces students to the fundamentals of web scraping and automation. By automating the process of navigating web pages, locating specific HTML elements, and downloading binary files, students learn how Python scripts interact with the modern web.

👨‍🏫 Instructor Facilitation Guide💻 Student Interactive Workbook



1. Module Overview & Learning Objectives
This project challenges students to build a functional web scraper that navigates the popular webcomic XKCD, extracts the daily comic, downloads the image file, and repeats the process automatically.
Core Learning Objectives: * Network Requests: Use the requests library to fetch HTML from a live URL. * HTML Parsing: Use BeautifulSoup (bs4) to navigate the Document Object Model (DOM) and extract specific elements using CSS selectors. * File I/O: Learn how to create directories and write binary data in chunks to save images locally. * Algorithmic Loops: Implement a while loop that dynamically updates its target URL to navigate backward through web pages.



2. Materials & Prerequisites

Software Environment: Python 3.x installed with the requests and beautifulsoup4 packages.
Platform: Quarto-rendered web pages hosted via Papillon Engineering or local Jupyter Notebooks.
Prior Knowledge: Basic understanding of HTML tags (<img>, <a>, id, href), Python while loops, and file paths.




3. Common Pitfalls & Instructor Key
If students attempt to run the original loop without updating the url variable at the end of the block, they will trigger an infinite loop, locking up their Python environment by downloading the same comic continuously.
Additionally, downloading all 3,000+ XKCD comics on a school network could trigger bandwidth throttles. The solution below includes a comics_to_download safety counter.
The Completed Solution Code:


Code
import requests, os, bs4

url = 'https://xkcd.com'               
os.makedirs('xkcd', exist_ok=True)    

comics_to_download = 5 # Safety limit for the classroom
count = 0

while not url.endswith('#') and count < comics_to_download:
    # 1. Download the page
    print(f'Downloading page {url}...')
    res = requests.get(url)
    res.raise_for_status()
    soup = bs4.BeautifulSoup(res.text, 'html.parser')

    # 2. Find the URL of the comic image
    comicElem = soup.select('#comic img')
    if comicElem == []:
        print('Could not find comic image.')
    else:
        comicUrl = 'https:' + comicElem[0].get('src')
        
        # 3. Download the image
        print(f'Downloading image {comicUrl}...')
        res = requests.get(comicUrl)
        res.raise_for_status()

        # 4. Save the image to ./xkcd
        imageFile = open(os.path.join('xkcd', os.path.basename(comicUrl)), 'wb')
        for chunk in res.iter_content(100000):
            imageFile.write(chunk)
        imageFile.close()

    # 5. Get the Prev button's url to update the loop
    prevLink = soup.select('a[rel="prev"]')[0]
    url = 'https://xkcd.com' + prevLink.get('href')
    count += 1

print('Done! Check your /xkcd folder.')






Introduction: Your Python Superpower
Imagine you want to download a picture from a website. You right-click, select “Save As”, and pick a folder. Easy, right? But what if you want to download every single picture from a website that has thousands of pages? Doing that by hand would take days.
Today, you are going to write a Python script that acts like an automated robot. It will visit the popular webcomic XKCD, find the daily comic, download it, click the “Previous” button, and do it all over again automatically.
Here is a classic XKCD comic about Python to show what we are grabbing:




Step 1: Setting up our Robot
We need three special tools for this job: requests (to browse the web), bs4 / BeautifulSoup (to read the website’s code), and os (to create folders on your computer).


Code
import requests, os, bs4

url = 'https://xkcd.com'               # The starting URL
os.makedirs('xkcd', exist_ok=True)     # Create a folder called 'xkcd' to store our images





Step 2: Fetching the Web Page
We will use a while loop to tell our robot to keep working. For this practice run, we will limit it to downloading just 5 comics so we don’t overload our network!


Code
comics_to_download = 5
count = 0

while not url.endswith('#') and count < comics_to_download:
    print(f'Downloading page {url}...')
    res = requests.get(url)
    res.raise_for_status() # This checks if the webpage actually loaded successfully
    
    # Translate the webpage text into readable HTML
    soup = bs4.BeautifulSoup(res.text, 'html.parser')





Step 3: Finding the Image
A web page is full of code. We need to tell our robot exactly where the comic is. If you right-click and “Inspect” the XKCD website, you will see the comic is always inside an HTML ID called comic, inside an img tag.


Code
    # Locate the image using a CSS Selector
    comicElem = soup.select('#comic img')
    
    if comicElem == []:
        print('Could not find comic image.')
    else:
        # Extract the image source URL
        comicUrl = 'https:' + comicElem[0].get('src')
        print(f'Found image at {comicUrl}... Downloading!')
        
        # Download the actual image file
        res = requests.get(comicUrl)
        res.raise_for_status()





Step 4: Saving the File (Binary Data)
Images aren’t text; they are “binary” data (1s and 0s). We need to open a file in “write binary” (wb) mode and save the image in small chunks so we don’t crash our computer’s memory.


Code
        # Create the file on your hard drive
        imageFile = open(os.path.join('xkcd', os.path.basename(comicUrl)), 'wb')
        
        # Save it in 100,000-byte chunks
        for chunk in res.iter_content(100000):
            imageFile.write(chunk)
        imageFile.close()





Step 5: Traveling Back in Time
If we stop here, our robot will just download today’s comic over and over forever! We need to find the “Prev” (Previous) button on the webpage, grab its link, and tell our robot to go there next.


Code
    # Find the "Previous" button link
    prevLink = soup.select('a[rel="prev"]')[0]
    
    # Update our main URL variable to the new page!
    url = 'https://xkcd.com' + prevLink.get('href')
    
    count += 1 # Increase our counter

print('Done! Check the new /xkcd folder on your computer.')





🚀 Project Challenge: Make it Your Own!
You just built a fully functional web scraper. But XKCD is just the beginning. How can you turn this script into your own unique project?
Brainstorming Ideas: 1. The Wallpaper Bot: Change the URL and CSS selectors to point to a high-res photography site (like Unsplash) and automatically download new desktop wallpapers. 2. The Weather Watcher: Set up a scraper to download the daily radar map image from a weather website to create a time-lapse of a storm. 3. The Sports Stat Tracker: Instead of finding an img tag, search for a <table> tag on a sports website to download your favorite player’s statistics into a text file.
Your Turn: Pick a website you visit often. Right-click, select “Inspect”, and see if you can figure out the CSS selectors for the data you care about. Then, adapt the code above to grab it!

title: Project 1: Introduction to Linear Regression
text:
Welcome to the Papillon Engineering K-12 Outreach Hub. This comprehensive module introduces students to data-driven engineering models through Simple Linear Regression, transitioning them from abstract algebraic line equations to active data science applications utilizing Python.

👨‍🏫 Instructor Facilitation Guide💻 Student Interactive Workbook



1. Module Overview & Learning Objectives
The purpose of this two-day module is to bridge the gap between standard high school algebra and professional engineering data analysis. Students will transition from solving standard y = mx + b problems on paper to utilizing modern Python libraries (numpy, pandas, plotly, and scikit-learn) to analyze real-world physical correlations.
Core Learning Objectives: * Mathematical Foundation: Define and interpret the slope (m) and y-intercept (b) in the context of real-world physical measurements (Height vs. Weight). * Data Visualization: Construct scatter plots and visualize linear trends using interactive Python graphics. * Algorithmic Calculation: Manually compute slope and intercept parameters using standard least-squares summation formulas. * Machine Learning Application: Implement professional industry frameworks to train a predictive regression model.



2. Materials & Prerequisites

Software Environment: Python 3.x installed with numpy, pandas, plotly, scikit-learn, and scipy packages.
Platform: Quarto-rendered web pages hosted via Papillon Engineering or local Jupyter Notebooks.
Prior Knowledge: Basic middle/high school algebra (equations of a line, PEMDAS) and elementary Python syntax (arrays and variable assignment).




3. Detailed Pacing Guide (120 Minutes Total)

Day 1: Theory, Data Inspection, and Visualization (60 Minutes)

Hook & Introduction (15 Mins): Engage students with real-world predictive questions. Do taller people systematically weigh more? How do engineers program autonomous systems to make predictions when sensor data has variability?
Mathematical Review (15 Mins): Introduce y = mx + b. Review what slope and intercept represent physically. Explain the concept of a “Line of Best Fit” minimizing error across a scattered dataset.
Loading Data & Pandas DataFrames (15 Mins): Guide students through initializing numpy arrays for height and weight. Explain the importance of structured data by formatting arrays into a tabular pandas.DataFrame.
Plotly Interactive Visualization (15 Mins): Execute the interactive scatter plot script. Teach students how to hover over data points, identify outliers, and visually confirm the positive correlation trend.



Day 2: Manual Calculations, Predictions, & Machine Learning (60 Minutes)

Least-Squares Math Breakdown (20 Mins): Walk through the algorithmic logic for calculating slope (m) and intercept (b). Emphasize that computers are simply executing algebraic summations extremely quickly.
Making Predictions (15 Mins): Use the derived linear equation to predict a target height. Instructor Prompt: Have students change the target height variable to their own height to predict their weight.
Industry Tools: Scikit-Learn & Scipy (15 Mins): Demonstrate how professional data scientists bypass manual algebraic code using linear_model.LinearRegression(). Discuss the concept of model “training” (fit).
Wrap-Up & Assessment (10 Mins): Review key takeaways. Assess student understanding by asking them to compare the manual calculation outputs with the scikit-learn outputs.





4. Assessment Strategies & Answer Key

Formative Check: Verify that students correctly reshape arrays (train_x = x.reshape(-1, 1)) when implementing scikit-learn. Explain that ML models expect 2D feature matrices, not 1D arrays.
Expected Output Reference:

Calculated Slope (m): 7.96
Calculated Intercept (b): -367.61
Predicted Weight for 69-inch height: 181.8 lbs






Introduction: We Are Learning About Models
Have you ever wondered if we can predict physical characteristics using math? In this module, our goal is to determine if there is a mathematical correlation between a person’s height and their weight. Generally, the taller someone is, the more likely they are to weigh more.
As engineers and data scientists, we can use Simple Linear Regression to build a mathematical model that accurately predicts a person’s weight for a given height based on historical data.



Step 1: Understanding the Data & Mathematical Foundations
In algebra, the equation of a straight line is written as:
y = mx + b

y: The dependent variable we want to predict (Weight in lbs).
x: The independent variable we already know (Height in inches).
m: The slope of the line (the rate of change, or how steep the line is).
b: The y-intercept (the starting value of y when x = 0).

Let’s start by loading our sample data into Python using the numpy (Numerical Python) and pandas (Data Analysis) libraries.


Code
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# x represents Heights (in inches)
x = np.array([66, 68, 60, 70, 65, 61, 74, 73, 75, 67])

# y represents Weights (in pounds)
y = np.array([160, 170, 110, 178, 155, 120, 223, 215, 235, 164])

# Display the data as a clean engineering table
data_table = pd.DataFrame({'Height (x)': x, 'Weight (y)': y})
data_table.head(10)

Step 2: Visualizing the Correlation
Before doing any complex math, engineers always plot their data to see if a relationship actually exists. We will use an interactive graphics library called plotly to visualize our height and weight data points.


Code
import plotly.express as px

# Create an interactive scatter plot
fig = px.scatter(
    x=x, y=y, 
    title="Height vs. Weight Correlation Analysis",
    labels={'x': 'Height (inches)', 'y': 'Weight (lbs)'},
    color_discrete_sequence=['#1c528b']
)

fig.update_layout(
    plot_bgcolor='white', 
    xaxis=dict(showgrid=True, gridcolor='lightgrey'), 
    yaxis=dict(showgrid=True, gridcolor='lightgrey')
)
fig.show()


                            
                                            








NoteObservation Check



Notice how the dots trend upward from left to right. This upward trajectory indicates a strong positive correlation between a person’s height and their weight.





Step 3: Calculating the Slope and Intercept Manually
To draw the perfect “Line of Best Fit” through these scattered data points, we need to calculate the exact slope (m) and intercept (b). We can program Python to do this using the Least-Squares summation formulas.


Code
# 1. Find the total number of data points
n = len(x)

# 2. Calculate the sums of x and y
sumx = np.sum(x)
sumy = np.sum(y)

# 3. Calculate product columns (x*y) and squared predictors (x^2)
multiplycolumxy = x * y
sum_multiplycolumxy = np.sum(multiplycolumxy)
x_squared = np.square(x)

# 4. Solve for the slope (m)
m = (n * sum_multiplycolumxy - sumx * sumy) / (n * np.sum(x_squared) - np.square(sumx))

# 5. Solve for the y-intercept (b)
b = (sumy * np.sum(x_squared) - sumx * sum_multiplycolumxy) / (n * np.sum(x_squared) - np.square(sumx))

print(f"Calculated Slope (m): {m:.2f}")
print(f"Calculated Intercept (b): {b:.2f}")


Calculated Slope (m): 7.96
Calculated Intercept (b): -367.61





Step 4: Making Real-World Predictions
Now that we have successfully solved for our line equation (y = 7.96x - 367.61), we can use it to make predictive estimations! Let’s predict the weight of someone who is 69 inches tall.


Code
# Predict weight for a target height of 69 inches
target_height = 69
predicted_weight = (m * target_height) + b

print(f"A person who is {target_height} inches tall is predicted to weigh {predicted_weight:.1f} lbs.")


A person who is 69 inches tall is predicted to weigh 181.8 lbs.


(Try changing the target_height variable in the code above to your own height in inches to see what the model predicts for you!)



Step 5: The Professional Way (Machine Learning Libraries)
In professional engineering and data science workflows, practitioners do not write out regression summation formulas line-by-line. Instead, we rely on robust Machine Learning libraries like scikit-learn or scientific modules like scipy to instantly train predictive models.
Here is how you accomplish the exact same prediction task using industry-standard tools:

Using Scikit-Learn


Code
from sklearn import linear_model

# Initialize the Machine Learning model
regr = linear_model.LinearRegression()

# Reshape the data (ML models require 2D arrays for features)
train_x = x.reshape(-1, 1)
train_y = y

# Train (fit) the model on our data
regr.fit(train_x, train_y)

print(f"Sklearn Slope: {regr.coef_[0]:.2f}")
print(f"Sklearn Intercept: {regr.intercept_:.2f}")


Sklearn Slope: 7.96
Sklearn Intercept: -367.61




Using Scipy (Numpy Polyfit)


Code
import scipy

# Calculate slope and intercept using polyfit (degree 1 for a straight line)
(mm, bb) = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)

print(f"Polyfit Slope: {mm:.2f}")
print(f"Polyfit Intercept: {bb:.2f}")


Polyfit Slope: 7.96
Polyfit Intercept: -367.61








TipProject Complete!



Notice that both professional ML tools returned the exact same slope (7.96) and intercept (-367.61) that we calculated manually from scratch. You have successfully built, verified, and implemented your first predictive machine learning model!

In engineering and applied sciences, the ability to rapidly analyze and visualize data is a critical skill. Whether you are optimizing a circuit, tracking the performance of an autonomous drone, or studying population growth, Python provides the tools to turn raw numbers into actionable insights.
In this introductory module, we will use Python to pull real-world data directly from the New York State government database, clean it, and build an interactive visualization of Suffolk County.

Step 1: Fetching the Data
Instead of downloading files manually, modern engineers use APIs (Application Programming Interfaces) to pull live data directly from the internet. We will use the urllib library to request the data, and pandas to organize it into a readable table called a DataFrame.


Code
import urllib.request
import json
import pandas as pd

# 1. Request data from the NY State API
url = 'https://data.ny.gov/resource/34dd-6g2j.json'
request = urllib.request.Request(url)
response = urllib.request.urlopen(request)

# 2. Parse the JSON response into a Pandas DataFrame
raw_data = response.read()
data_json = json.loads(raw_data)
df = pd.json_normalize(data_json)

title: Introduction to Python for STEM
text:
Bonus: Engineering Math Functions
Python is also a powerful calculator. When designing cylindrical tanks for sustainable aviation fuel, we frequently need to calculate the area of a circle.
Note: In Python, exponents are written using two asterisks (**), not a caret (^).


Code
import math

def calculate_circle_area(radius):
    """Calculates the area of a circle given its radius."""
    area = (radius ** 2) * math.pi
    print(f"The area of a circle with a radius of {radius} is: {area:.2f}")

# Test the function with a radius of 5
calculate_circle_area(5)


The area of a circle with a radius of 5 is: 78.54

title: RF Fox Hunt & Transient Telemetry Lab
text:
What is a Fox Hunt?
A “Fox Hunt” (officially called Amateur Radio Direction Finding, or ARDF) is a classic engineering game. One person hides a small, battery-powered radio transmitter (the “Fox”) somewhere in a building or park. The rest of the teams (the “Hunters”) must use their knowledge of signal strength, decibels (\text{dBm}), and directional antennas (like our Pringles Cantenna) to track down the hidden transmitter.
To play, we first need to build our Fox. Today, you will program a Raspberry Pi to act as a standalone Wi-Fi beacon that automatically starts broadcasting the moment you plug in a battery!

title: RF Fox Hunt & Transient Telemetry Lab
text:
What is a Wi-Fi Beacon?
Every wireless router in the world constantly shouts an invisible radio packet into the air about 10 times every single second. This packet is called a Beacon Frame. It contains the network’s name (the SSID) so your phone knows the network exists.
Even if you don’t type in the password to connect to the network, your phone’s Wi-Fi antenna can still feel the physical power of the Beacon Frame hitting it. We will measure that power (the RSSI in \text{dBm}) to play our game.

title: RF Fox Hunt & Transient Telemetry Lab
text:
Step 1: Creating the Beacon
We will use nmcli (NetworkManager Command Line Interface) to command the Raspberry Pi’s internal wireless chip to stop acting like a normal computer and start acting like a wireless router.

Open the terminal on your Raspberry Pi.
Type the following command exactly as written, then press Enter:

sudo nmcli device wifi hotspot ifname wlan0 band bg channel 11 ssid The_Hidden_Fox password catchmeifyoucan
What did we just do? * ifname wlan0: Tells the Pi to use its built-in Wi-Fi antenna. * band bg channel 11: Forces the transmitter to use the 2.462\,\text{GHz} frequency (a long enough wavelength to measure easily). * ssid The_Hidden_Fox: This is the network name the Hunters will look for!

title: RF Fox Hunt & Transient Telemetry Lab
section: Step 2: Making the Beacon “Persistent” (Auto-Start on Boot)
text:
Step 2: Making the Beacon “Persistent” (Auto-Start on Boot)
If we hide the Raspberry Pi in a backpack or above a ceiling tile, we won’t have a screen or keyboard to type commands. The Pi must automatically start shouting its beacon the instant we plug it into a portable USB battery bank.
When we ran the command in Step 1, NetworkManager saved our new beacon as a connection profile named Hotspot. We need to modify this profile so it automatically connects on boot with the highest priority.

Tell the Pi to auto-connect to the Hotspot profile:

sudo nmcli connection modify Hotspot connection.autoconnect yes

Give the Hotspot a high priority (so the Pi chooses to be a beacon instead of trying to connect to the school’s normal Wi-Fi):

sudo nmcli connection modify Hotspot connection.autoconnect-priority 100

The Ultimate Fallback: Using Cron Sometimes, NetworkManager gets confused if it sees familiar networks nearby. To absolutely guarantee our Fox wakes up howling, we can add a scheduling rule to the Linux cron system. This tells the operating system to force the Hotspot on every time the computer boots up.
Type crontab -e in the terminal (select nano if it asks for an editor). Scroll all the way to the bottom of the file and add this exact line:
@reboot sleep 10 && nmcli connection up Hotspot
Press Ctrl+O (then Enter) to save, and **Ctrl+Xto exit. Thesleep 10` command gives the Wi-Fi chip 10 seconds to warm up before firing the beacon command.

title: RF Fox Hunt & Transient Telemetry Lab
text:
Step 3: Test Your Fox
Let’s make sure it works! 1. Restart your Raspberry Pi by typing sudo reboot in the terminal. 2. Wait 60 seconds for the Pi to fully boot up. 3. Take out your smartphone, go to your Wi-Fi settings, and look at the list of available networks. 4. If you see The_Hidden_Fox in the list, congratulations! Your beacon is actively broadcasting.

title: RF Fox Hunt & Transient Telemetry Lab
text:
Lab Instructions: The Fox Hunt
In this lab, you will use your directional waveguide to detect a hidden 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi signal broadcasted by a Raspberry Pi 5. By measuring the Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) in decibel-milliwatts (\text{dBm}), you will triangulate the physical origin of the signal.

Step-by-Step Procedure

Connect the Hardware: Plug the USB Wi-Fi adapter into your laptop. Ensure the adapter is mounted securely inside the uncut Pringles can waveguide.
Launch the Terminal: Open a new terminal window on your laptop.
Select a Tracking Method: Choose one of the exploration methods below.
Find the Peak Signal: Stand at your assigned station and slowly rotate the cantenna 360^\circ. The signal is at its strongest (peak) when the negative number gets closest to zero.
Log the Vector: When you find the peak value, use a smartphone compass to record the exact heading the open end of the cantenna is pointing.



Exploration Method 1: Quick Radar (Terminal)
This command refreshes your screen every 0.5 seconds, turning your terminal into a live radar dashboard without saving the data. Press Ctrl+C to stop.
watch -n 0.5 "iwconfig wlan0 | grep -i 'signal level'"


Exploration Method 2: Data Logging (Python)
For advanced analysis, this script continuously logs the RSSI values to a CSV file along with precise timestamps. Save this as waveguide_telemetry.py and run it:
import subprocess, time, csv

INTERFACE = "wlan0"
OUTPUT_FILE = "waveguide_telemetry.csv"

def get_rssi():
    cmd = f"iwconfig {INTERFACE} | grep -i --color=never 'signal level'"
    res = subprocess.check_output(cmd, shell=True).decode("utf-8")
    for part in res.split():
        if "level=" in part:
            return float(part.split("=")[1])
    return -100.0

print("Logging RSSI (dBm)... Press Ctrl+C to stop.")
with open(OUTPUT_FILE, "w", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["Timestamp_s", "RSSI_dBm"])
    t0 = time.time()
    while True:
        rssi = get_rssi()
        elapsed = round(time.time() - t0, 2)
        print(f"t = {elapsed:5.2f} s | Signal = {rssi:6.1f} dBm")
        writer.writerow([elapsed, rssi])
        time.sleep(0.5)

title: RF Fox Hunt & Transient Telemetry Lab
text:
Data Acquisition: DC Transient Telemetry
The analog RC circuit connects directly to an ADS1115 16-Bit ADC, which communicates with the Raspberry Pi 5 over the \text{I}^2\text{C} bus.

I2C Bus & Power Wiring:

Red Wire: VDD (3.3V Power)
Blue Wire: SDA (Data Line to GPIO 2)
Orange Wire: SCL (Clock Line to GPIO 3)
Black Wire: Common System Ground



Software Implementation: ADS1115 Data Logging
Once the physical circuit is wired, use this script to record capacitor voltage over time to a CSV file:
import time
import board
import busio
import csv
import adafruit_ads1x15.ads1115 as ADS
from adafruit_ads1x15.analog_in import AnalogIn

i2c = busio.I2C(board.SCL, board.SDA)
adc = ADS.ADS1115(i2c)
chan = AnalogIn(adc, ADS.P0)

print("Logging RC Voltage to CSV... Press Ctrl+C to stop.")
with open("rc_transient_data.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["Time_s", "Voltage_V"])
    
    t0 = time.time()
    while True:
        elapsed = round(time.time() - t0, 3)
        volts = round(chan.voltage, 3)
        print(f"t = {elapsed:5.3f} s | V_c = {volts} V")
        writer.writerow([elapsed, volts])
        time.sleep(0.05)

title: RF Fox Hunt & Transient Telemetry Lab
text:
Assembly Notes & Instructor Guidelines

Ground Referencing: The analog breadboard ground, the oscilloscope ground, and the Raspberry Pi digital ground must share a common reference, otherwise the ADC will read floating, erratic voltage values.
Time Constant (\tau): For R = 10\,\text{k}\Omega and C = 100\,\mu\text{F}, the theoretical time constant is \tau = RC = 1.0 second. In the DC circuit, the capacitor reaches approximately 63.2\% of V_{in} after 1.0 second.
